questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following terms.

(i) Solubility

(ii) Solubility curve *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Solubility** is the **mass of a solute that dissolves in 100 g of water (the solvent) to form a saturated solution at a given temperature** (unit: g per 100 g of water).

(ii) A **solubility curve** is a graph showing how the solubility of a substance varies with temperature (solubility on the vertical axis, temperature on the horizontal axis).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The table below gives the solubility of potassium nitrate ($\mathrm{KNO_3}$) in grams per 100 g of water at different temperatures.

| Temperature in $^\circ$C | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Solubility of $\mathrm{KNO_3}$ in g per 100 g of $\mathrm{H_2O}$ | 16 | 21 | 31 | 45 | 62 | 81 | 106 |

Plot the solubility of $\mathrm{KNO_3}$ against temperature (X-axis). *[10 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
*(The learner draws the graph on graph paper.)*

- **Axes:** temperature in $^\circ$C on the X-axis, from 0 to 60 (for example 1 cm for 5 $^\circ$C or 2 cm for 10 $^\circ$C); solubility in g per 100 g of water on the Y-axis, from 0 to 110 (for example 1 cm for 10 g). Label both axes with units and give the graph a title.
- **Points to plot:** (0, 16), (10, 21), (20, 31), (30, 45), (40, 62), (50, 81), (60, 106). Mark each with a cross or a small circle.
- **Curve:** join the points with a **smooth curve** (not straight segments). The curve rises slowly and then more and more steeply: solubility increases with temperature, and the curve is concave upwards.

The values used in the next parts are read from this curve.

(i) At 45 $^\circ$C, read up from 45 $^\circ$C to the curve, then across to the solubility axis: about **71 g per 100 g of water** (between 62 g at 40 $^\circ$C and 81 g at 50 $^\circ$C; a straight-line estimate gives 71.5 g, and a value between 70 g and 72 g is acceptable).

(ii) Read across from 40 g on the solubility axis to the curve, then down to the temperature axis: about **27 $^\circ$C** (between 20 $^\circ$C, 31 g, and 30 $^\circ$C, 45 g; values from 26 $^\circ$C to 28 $^\circ$C are acceptable).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) What mass of $\mathrm{KNO_3}$ would be obtained when a saturated solution is cooled from 50 $^\circ$C to 15 $^\circ$C?

(ii) Calculate the amount of substance of $\mathrm{KNO_3}$ in mol found in 100 g of water in (d)(i) above. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) A saturated solution holds 81 g of $\mathrm{KNO_3}$ per 100 g of water at 50 $^\circ$C. From the curve the solubility at 15 $^\circ$C is about 26 g per 100 g of water (between 21 g at 10 $^\circ$C and 31 g at 20 $^\circ$C). The excess crystallises out:

mass of crystals $= 81 - 26 = 55\ \mathrm{g}$ (per 100 g of water)

**Answer: about 55 g** (values from 54 g to 56 g are acceptable).

(ii) Molar mass of $\mathrm{KNO_3} = 39 + 14 + 3 \times 16 = 101\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

amount of substance $= \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}} = \dfrac{55}{101} = 0.54\ \mathrm{mol}$

**Answer: about 0.54 mol.**

questions.enonce_markdown: State one use of solubility curves. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown: Solubility curves are used to **find the mass of a salt that will crystallise out when a saturated solution is cooled** (hence to choose the best conditions for crystallisation and purification of a salt). They are also used to read the solubility of a substance at any temperature and to compare the solubilities of different substances.
